title-slide.en: Welcome to session four, the first session on Markov analysis.
Today we model CellCo's cell line as a Markov chain, estimate its transition matrix from data, and test whether the night shift behaves like the day shift.

route.en: Here is the plan for the next two hours.
First, states, transition matrices and the steady state, followed by a dice activity in which you play the cell line.
After the break, we estimate a transition matrix from a log, put intervals on it, and test the night shift. The session ends with the launch of the group assignment.

states.en: In every shift, CellCo records the state of its cell line: running, slow or down.
A Markov chain assumes that the next state depends only on the current state, not on the history before it.
The transition matrix holds the probability of moving from each state, in the row, to each state, in the column. Each row adds up to one.
For example, a running line stays running in four shifts out of six, and breaks down in one out of six. The values are sixths so that a die can play the line in the first activity.

n-step.en: To find where the line will be after n shifts, multiply the starting distribution by the matrix n times.
Starting from down, the chance of running is 0.5 after one shift, 0.58 after two, and 0.60 after four.
After about four shifts, the line forgets where it started. The long-run distribution is the steady state, which solves pi equals pi times P.
Here the line runs 60 percent of shifts in the long run. If a slow shift makes half the cells, throughput is 70 percent of capacity.

n-explorer.en: Choose a starting state and move the slider to change the number of shifts.
The bars show the probability of each state, and the dashed lines show the steady state.
Whatever the starting state, the bars reach the dashed lines within a few shifts.

readings.en: The steady state answers practical questions.
The line returns to down every five shifts on average, which is one over 0.2.
Once it is running, it stays running for three shifts on average, which is one over one minus four sixths.
And at 70 percent effective throughput, a line rated at 2 gigawatt hours per year delivers about 1.4. That links directly to the demand numbers we used in sessions one to three.

act1.en: Activity one. You are the cell line.
Start in running and roll your die ten times. The rules on the slide tell you the next state for each roll. Write down your state after every roll.
Count your transitions and add them to the table on the board.
Then, in pairs, estimate each transition probability from the class total, and compare it with the true sixths. Finally, check what share of all shifts was running, and compare it with 0.6.

estimate.en: To estimate a transition matrix from a log, count the moves out of each state and divide by the number of visits to that state. This is the maximum-likelihood estimate.
Each estimate has a standard error, and an approximate 95 percent interval is the estimate plus or minus 1.96 standard errors.
In the day shift's log, the line left running 635 times and stayed running 448 times. So the estimate is 0.706, with an interval from 0.67 to 0.74.
Rows that are visited rarely have wide intervals. The down row was visited only 189 times, and its standard error is about twice that of the running row.

sample-explorer.en: This widget simulates a log of the chosen length and estimates every row with its 95 percent interval.
Move the slider from thirty shifts to thirty thousand, and draw new logs to see how much the estimates move.
Ten times more data makes the interval about three times narrower, because the standard error falls with the square root of the number of visits.

homogeneity.en: Is the night shift different? Here are a thousand logged shifts from each.
For each starting state, a chi-square test compares the day and night counts. The three test statistics add up to 20.55, with 6 degrees of freedom, and a p-value of 0.002.
So one matrix does not fit both shifts.
The difference sits in the running row. By night, a running line breaks down in 23 percent of shifts, against 15 percent by day.

act2.en: Activity two. Work in pairs for fifteen minutes.
Estimate the probability that a running line breaks down, separately for the day and the night shift, with 95 percent intervals.
Then compare the steady states of the two matrices, and estimate how many more shifts per thousand the night line would run if it behaved like the day line.
Finish with one sentence for the plant manager on what the night shift should investigate first.

act2-answer.en: By day, the breakdown probability from running is 0.150, plus or minus 0.028. By night it is 0.231, plus or minus 0.036. The intervals do not overlap.
The day matrix runs 63.5 percent of shifts in the long run, the night matrix 52.8 percent. Matching the day shift would add about 107 running shifts per thousand.
The night shift should investigate why running shifts break down: the maintenance handover, staffing, or start-up after a planned stop.

assignment.en: Now the group assignment for block one.
Groups of four to five write a board memo for CellCo, due on the twenty-first of February 2027.
It has three parts: a decision analysis, a Markov analysis of your group's own log, and a network plan for the chosen option.

The deliverables are a report of at most ten pages, a workbook or notebook, and a ten-minute recorded presentation. Each student also writes a two-page research note applying one method to their own research.

debrief.en: A Markov chain is a transition matrix. The steady state solves pi equals pi times P, and CellCo's line runs 60 percent of shifts in the long run.
Estimate each row as counts divided by visits, and report its interval. Rarely visited states have the widest intervals.
And test whether one matrix fits all conditions before you use it. CellCo's night shift breaks down more often.
Tomorrow, session five uses absorbing chains to compute yield, rework and scrap on the cell line.

exit.en: For the exit ticket, explain in one sentence to a production engineer why two hundred logged shifts are not enough to estimate the down row precisely.
Remember that quiz one opens online this evening.
